meta.title: When to Trim Hedges in Michigan, by Plant | HD Landscape
meta.description: Shape Michigan hedges in late spring to early summer, do hard cuts in early spring and stop by mid-summer. Timing for boxwood, yew and arborvitae, by plant.

title: When to trim hedges **in Michigan.**
lede: Most Michigan hedges get their main shaping trim in late spring or early summer, once the new growth has filled out. Hard cuts belong in early spring, and cutting stops by mid-summer. Boxwood, yew and arborvitae each have their own quirks.
short: Shape clipped evergreen hedges in late spring to early summer, roughly May into June, after the new growth fills out.
Save heavy cuts for early spring, before new growth starts.
Stop hard cutting by mid-summer. Late growth may not harden off before winter.
Yew can take a hard cut back into old wood. Arborvitae cannot, so stay in the green.
Keep the top narrower than the base, or the bottom of the hedge goes bare.

sections.h: Cut hard in early spring, shape by June, stop by mid-summer
p: Michigan State University Extension says many shrubs do well pruned in late winter or early spring, before new growth starts. Wisconsin and Penn State extension say the same for clipped evergreens, and add a later trim for shape. Iowa State University Extension's calendar starts shearing evergreen hedges in May through early June, just after the new flush of growth, and says to avoid extensive pruning after mid-summer.

sections.h: Three common hedges, three different limits
p: Boxwood, yew and arborvitae are three of the most common clipped hedges, and each one wants something a little different.

sections.h: How far back you can cut depends on the plant
p: The calendars run close together. How hard you can cut is where the plants part ways.
list: **Boxwood** is a light touch plant. Trim it when it is dry, since boxwood blight spreads on dirty tools and splashing water.

**Yew** is the forgiving one. Among needled evergreens like arborvitae and juniper, Penn State Extension says only yews have dormant buds on old wood, so a hard cut can bring one back. Wisconsin says not to be afraid to cut a large overgrown yew back considerably, and to leave some small shoots on the limbs you cut. Expect it to look rough for a while.

**Arborvitae** is a shaping plant, and Wisconsin says pruning it is usually for minor shaping, not major downsizing. It handles regular trims well as long as you stay in the green. Penn State says a cut back to bare brown wood will not regrow, and that branch will die.
**Junipers** are the exception to shearing. Wisconsin says junipers and false cypress should not be sheared or cut back to older, non-leafy areas, because new growth takes years to hide the cuts.
**Lilac and forsythia** run on a different clock. They set their flower buds the summer before, so MSU says to wait until right after they bloom. A trim in early spring cuts off the flowers.
after: A tall arborvitae hedge cannot simply be cut down to half its height and left to green up. Tell Jake how tall you want it, and he can say how far it will safely come down. There is more on tall and overgrown hedges under [hedge trimming](/hedge-trimming/).
One safety note: Penn State says yew berries and foliage are poisonous to people and pets, which is one more reason to clean up the clippings.

sections.h: Why hard cutting stops by mid-summer
p: Pruning pushes new growth, and growth that starts late in the season may not harden off before winter. University of Minnesota Extension says arborvitae, junipers, yews and hemlocks can be pruned until mid-summer. University of Wisconsin Extension says not to prune junipers and false cypress after August, for that same reason.

Fall is the wrong time for a hard cut, even if the hedge looks shaggy. Iowa State says fall pruned evergreens are more open to winter injury. If it has to look sharp for an event or a sale, ask Jake what a light tidy can do without setting the plant back. Our [fall cleanup checklist](/journal/fall-cleanup-checklist-michigan/) covers what to do instead.

sections.h: Keep the top narrower than the bottom
p: A hedge should be wider at the base than at the top. MSU, Penn State, Wisconsin and Minnesota extension all say so, because the slant lets sun reach the lower branches. Penn State describes the shape as an inverted V, and the top can be flat, rounded or pointed.

A hedge that is bare at the bottom usually got that way from a top wider than its base, which shades out the lower branches. The slant does not need to be dramatic. A slight taper is hard to notice from the sidewalk, and the bottom of the hedge will show the difference.

sections.h: A formal hedge needs at least two trims a year
p: Iowa State University Extension says a formal evergreen hedge needs pruning at least twice a year, and that the tidiest hedges take it almost monthly. University of Minnesota Extension's version is spring and again in mid-summer. Penn State's is early spring with an optional light pass in summer. A loose, unsheared hedge needs far less.
We can do a one time trim, or work your hedges into [monthly landscape maintenance](/monthly-landscape-maintenance/).

sections.h: Brown patches: look before you cut
p: Brown on a Michigan hedge can mean a few different things, and they do not all get the same fix.
list: **Winter damage.** Wait for spring. Once new growth starts, a hedge can be pruned back to living shoots, and branches broken by snow get cut out clean.

**Boxwood blight.** A fungal disease first found in Michigan in 2018. MSU says it can look like other problems, so have a sample checked by MSU Plant and Pest Diagnostics before you decide anything. Clean your tools between plants.

**Box tree moth.** An invasive insect whose caterpillars chew boxwood leaves and leave webbing. Macomb, Oakland and Wayne counties are all inside Michigan's quarantine, which bars moving boxwood out of the area, clippings included.
